content: Adults are strongly encouraged to engage in regular physical activity, as it provides numerous health benefits. It is recommended that adults perform at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity, or an equivalent combination of both intensities throughout the week to achieve substantial health benefits. Evidence supports that even some physical activity is better than none, and individuals who are not meeting these recommendations can still improve their health by engaging in any amount of physical activity.g., reduced adiposity). For additional health benefits, adults may increase their moderate-intensity aerobic activity to more than 300 minutes per week or their vigorous-intensity activity to more than 150 minutes per week, or a combination of both. In addition to aerobic activity, adults should engage in muscle-strengthening activities of moderate or greater intensity that involve all major muscle groups on two or more days per week, as these provide additional health benefits. Limiting sedentary behavior is also crucial, as replacing sedentary time with physical activity of any intensity, including light activity, can improve health outcomes. Older adults (aged 65 years and older) are similarly advised to engage in regular physical activity, with the same recommendations for aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities. Older adults should also incorporate multicomponent physical activities that emphasize functional balance and strength training at moderate or greater intensity on three or more days per week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. Starting with small amounts of physical activity and gradually increasing frequency, intensity, and duration over time is recommended for those who are less active. Higher levels of sedentary behavior in older adults are linked to poor health outcomes, including increased mortality from all causes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer, as well as a higher incidence of type-2 diabetes and other chronic conditions. Pregnant and postpartum women without contraindications are advised to engage in regular physical activity throughout pregnancy and postpartum. At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week is recommended, along with a variety of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities. Gentle stretching may also be beneficial. Physical activity during pregnancy and postpartum is associated with reduced risks of pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes, excessive weight gain, delivery complications, and postpartum depression, as well as fewer newborn complications. It does not adversely affect birth weight or increase the risk of stillbirth. Pregnant women should avoid activities involving physical contact, a high risk of falling, or those that may limit oxygenation (e.g., high-altitude activities for those unaccustomed to such environments). Activities in the supine position should be avoided after the first trimester. Hydration and avoiding excessive heat during exercise are also important considerations. Adults and older adults with chronic conditions, such as cancer survivors, individuals with hypertension, type-2 diabetes, or HIV, should also engage in regular physical activity. For these populations, physical activity improves outcomes such as reduced all-cause mortality, disease-specific mortality, and disease progression, as well as enhanced physical function, mental health, and quality of life. At least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week is recommended, with additional benefits from exceeding these levels. Muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups on two or more days per week are also advised. Multicomponent physical activities that emphasize balance and strength training on three or more days per week are particularly beneficial for older adults with chronic conditions to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. For individuals unable to meet these recommendations, any amount of physical activity according to their abilities is beneficial. Starting with small amounts and gradually increasing activity levels is encouraged. Consulting with a healthcare provider or physical activity specialist may help tailor activities to individual needs, abilities, and medical conditions. Pre-exercise medical clearance is generally unnecessary for lightor moderate-intensity activities, such as brisk walking, unless contraindications are present.
